Official SpamZilla plans

What is SpamZilla used for?

SpamZilla helps you narrow a list of expired or expiring domains to candidates you can review by hand. A list may contain more names than you have time to research. Filters can help remove names outside your topic, budget, or preferred extension. Once you have a shortlist, spend most of your time on history, links, and whether the name still fits a genuine website.

A freelance SEO might use it to review names for a client project. A site owner might use it to look for a memorable domain with a relevant history. An agency might use it to compare candidates across several projects. In each case, the useful outcome is a short decision list with evidence and open questions.

The domain research tool and the purchase venue are different parts of the process. A result can point you to a name that is expiring, available, or listed for sale elsewhere. Check the current status and terms with the registrar or marketplace before paying. A domain may sell, renew, or change status while a research report is still available.

Start with the purpose of the website

Before you open the database, write one sentence about the site you would build. For example, you might want a public guide to repairing commuter bicycles in one city. A domain that once hosted a cycling community could be worth checking. A similarly priced domain that used to cover an unrelated topic may offer a name you like, but its previous audience may have little reason to use the new site.

Write down the name requirements, preferred extension, language, and budget. Consider whether you could explain the name easily to a customer and whether people are likely to spell it correctly. Include the maximum renewal cost you are willing to pay. A short list of requirements gives you a reason to rule out names that look attractive in a report but would be awkward to use in practice.

Check for naming conflicts before committing. Search for active businesses with similar names in the market you want to serve, and verify any trademark concern through the relevant official records or qualified advice. Domain availability alone does not resolve naming rights. If a candidate would rely on an existing brand to attract visits, choose a name that can stand on its own.

Review the domain’s history

Look at archived snapshots from several periods where they are available. Check the home page and a few internal pages. Read the headings and navigation to see who the site served and whether the topic changed. A consistent archive can help explain the links you find later. Missing snapshots leave a gap in the evidence, so record what you could check and which dates are missing.

Pay attention to abrupt changes. A cycling site that later carried unrelated sales pages deserves closer inspection. An archive may also show legitimate changes, such as a business rebrand or a move from a blog to a product site. Record the dates and compare the archive with the links people used at the time. That helps you distinguish ordinary changes from a pattern that does not fit your project.

Check current behavior as well. Open the address if it is safe to do so and see whether it leads to a live site, a parked page, a sale listing, or another domain. Compare that result with what the research tool and the purchase venue say. If the domain points to a different business or its ownership status is unclear, resolve the discrepancy before relying on the candidate.

Check backlinks by opening source pages

A backlink report gives you a list of places that linked to a domain. Choose a sample that includes relevant sites, unusual anchor text, and links to different parts of the old website. Open the source pages where possible and read the text around the links. The reason a page linked to the domain can tell you more than the total number of links.

For a cycling domain, an old local club might link to an event calendar or a route map. Ask whether the destination still exists and whether you can offer a current resource for that audience. A link from a genuine article is useful evidence of past relevance. It does not tell you whether the author will keep the link or whether people still visit the page.

Look at how many links come from different sites and how the links are placed. A long list can include repeated links from one template or directory. A smaller set can include sites closely related to the project you want to build. Keep a note of the pages you checked and the context you found, especially when one or two links are the main reason a domain interests you. For a separate link research workflow, compare Majestic Group Buy.

Use automated spam checks as review prompts

An automated score can help you decide which candidates to inspect first. It summarizes the signals that the tool found. A low score does not guarantee that every part of the domain’s history is clean. A high score does not explain which links, anchor text, or previous pages created the concern. Open sample pages and record specific evidence before making a decision.

Look for patterns that are difficult to explain through the site’s previous purpose. Examples include repeated commercial anchors unrelated to the archived topic, links from many similar low-value pages, or several sudden changes in what the site offered. A single odd link can happen to a legitimate site. A pattern across the archive and referring pages is a better reason to investigate or choose another candidate.

Set an evidence threshold before buying. For example, you might require a relevant name, a history you can explain, several verifiable links from related pages, and clear ownership and renewal terms. If an important item cannot be checked, mark it as unknown. A candidate with unknown history may still have value as a name, but price it for that use rather than assuming its former visibility will return.

Work through an example shortlist

Imagine you have three possible names for a commuter bicycle repair site. The first has the best-looking metric, but its archive jumps from cycling to unrelated promotions and most of its visible links come from the same directory. The second has a relevant name and a few links from local cycling articles, but the price is higher. The third has a clean, memorable name and little past activity.

Review them against the planned site. If the strongest reason to buy the first name is the metric, ask which specific reader, link, or feature would benefit your project. If you cannot identify one, that candidate may be less useful than it first appears. For the second, open several sources and check whether the previous pages match something you can realistically create. For the third, compare its registration and renewal costs with a new name.

Write down what would change your decision. You might choose the second if its sale and renewal terms fit the budget and the relevant source pages are still accessible. You might choose the third if the project mainly needs a recognizable brand. You might pass on all three if none offers a clear advantage over registering a fresh domain. The shortlist has done its job when you know why you would buy or walk away.

Compare discounted access and official plans

Check the access period, price at checkout, and the limits of the actual SEOGBTools offer. If your workflow depends on importing a list, looking at backlink details, saving filters, or exporting results, ask about those exact actions. Also check how usage limits apply to the feature you need. A plan that works for two candidates may not fit a weekly review of many domains.

Compare the research cost with the rest of the project. Include the domain price, any auction or transfer fee, renewal, hosting, and time to build or maintain useful content. If the purchase only makes sense when the old domain produces immediate search traffic, reconsider the assumptions. An old domain can be an asset you can use, but its past search performance is no guarantee of future visits.

Test a small example using public information. Find one candidate, inspect a sample of history and backlinks, and check whether you can save a useful record. Then look up the domain at its purchase venue and verify the current status and price. This gives you a better comparison than a feature list alone. If you also need a crawler to audit a website you own, see Screaming Frog Group Buy.

Keep a record before you bid

Use a short spreadsheet with the domain name, purchase venue, asking price, renewal cost, historical topic, sample link sources, and unresolved questions. Add the date of every check. Domains can change status quickly, so verify the live purchase terms again before placing a bid. Keep the link evidence separate from any score so someone else can reproduce the decision.

For a team purchase, assign one person to confirm the domain is going into the right registrar account. Verify who will control the registration and how renewals will be handled. If the domain is for a client, agree on ownership before buying. An account or billing mix-up can make a good name difficult to use later.

Once you own a domain, build the site for the audience you identified. Keep useful content and navigation easy to find. If you plan to reuse old paths, map them only where a new page serves the same purpose. Review Google’s spam policies on expired domain abuse before choosing a strategy.

Frequently asked questions

Does SpamZilla sell the domains in the results?

Check the listing to see where the name can be registered, bought, or bid on. Research access and buying the domain are separate costs. Confirm availability and purchase terms with the relevant venue before paying.

Does an older domain automatically rank better?

Domain age alone does not tell you whether the new site will earn search traffic. Review past use, links, current demand, and what you can build for the reader. Compare the domain with a fresh registration that fits the same purpose.

How many backlinks should I inspect?

Start with a representative sample across different referring sites, anchors, and destinations. Check the most relevant links and any examples that look out of place. Expand the sample if the first pass raises a question that could change the decision.

Is SpamZilla group buy access enough for occasional research?

It depends on the current offer and how you work. Check the available searches, credits, exports, and access period. Run a small public test and compare it with the official options before relying on it for a client deadline.

What should I do if there is no archive history?

Record that the previous use could not be verified. Review what you can learn from current status and referring pages, then decide whether the name alone justifies the cost. Avoid paying a premium based on a history you cannot confirm.
